body.en: William Saroyan (1908–1981) was an American *writer* born to Armenian immigrant parents, and many of his stories draw on that community in rural California. This story is told by Aram, a nine-year-old boy, looking back on one summer of his childhood. The family is very poor, but it is proud of its name.

narration.en: Let us place the family at the centre and draw each character around it.

say.en: At the centre is the Garoghlanian family: very poor, but famous for honesty.
Aram, nine years old, tells the story.
Mourad, his thirteen-year-old cousin, has a magical way with horses.
Uncle Khosrove is loud and short-tempered, and waves problems away.
John Byro, an Assyrian farmer, owns the white horse.
And the beautiful white horse is the joy of that summer.

problem.en: Why is the Garoghlanian family's reputation important in the story?

steps.en: State the reputation: the family is poor but famous for honesty.
Link to the plot: John Byro cannot believe the boys would steal.
Outcome: his trust makes the boys return the horse.

answer.en: The Garoghlanians were poor but famous for honesty. Because of this, John Byro refused to believe the boys had stolen his horse, and his trust made them feel bound to return it, so the reputation shapes the ending.
